---
title: "Communication, Meetings, and Digital Body Language"
---

{#sec-communication}

Most of our work — and most of our misunderstandings — happen in writing, across channels, often asynchronously. This chapter sets our communication norms so that "where is that file?" and "who owns this task?" stop being productivity leaks, and so our written tone builds trust rather than eroding it.

## Channels: one job per channel

We use several streams, each with a clear purpose. If communication styles differ across the group, we revisit these after a trial period rather than forcing one channel to do everything.

| Channel | Use it for | Don't use it for |
|---|---|---|
| **Project management tool** (e.g., ClickUp / GitHub Projects) | Tasks, owners, due dates, status | Long discussions, file storage |
| **GitHub Issues** | Code, bugs, analysis questions, manual edits | Sensitive data, personnel matters |
| **Google Drive / OneDrive** | Documents, drafts, shared materials | Code (use GitHub), raw restricted data |
| **Messaging channel** (single primary tool) | Quick updates, human connection, "I'm stuck" | Decisions of record (move those to a tracked tool) |
| **Email** | External communication, formal records | Day-to-day internal coordination |
| **Video (Zoom / Meet)** | Meetings, working sessions, recorded discussions | Things better handled async in writing |

::: {.callout-important}
## The "single source of truth" rule
Every task, decision, and document has **one** home. Tasks live in the project tool; code and code-discussion live in GitHub; documents live in the shared drive. When a decision happens in chat or a meeting, **record it in the tracked tool.** If it isn't written down somewhere findable, it didn't happen.
:::

## Which name represents which work

External communication must attribute work to the correct entity
(@sec-entity-structure). Getting this wrong can wrongly imply that Lynn University
endorses the entire Institute, or blur a separately incorporated entity into
RIPLRT.

| Context | Name to use | Handle |
|---|---|---|
| Institute-level research, mentoring, recruitment | **RIPLRT Institute** | @riplrt / riplrt.com |
| Work conducted within Lynn University | **Educational Biomarker Discovery Lab**, with the member's Lynn affiliation | per Lynn comms norms |
| Bilingual science-communication content | **Vistazo A La Ciencia** (a *separate* LLC, not RIPLRT) | @vistazoalaciencia |
| Personal commentary by the PI | personal capacity, not the Institute | @friveramariani |

Rules of the road:

- **Never state or imply that the RIPLRT Institute is a Lynn University unit.** It is a DBA of Felix E. Rivera-Mariani, PhD, LLC.
- Use the **EBDL** name only for Lynn-housed work, and follow Lynn University branding and approval norms whenever Lynn is named.
- Keep **Vistazo A La Ciencia** distinct — it is a different entity with its own mission, not a RIPLRT channel.
- When in doubt about a public post, logo, or co-branding, clear it with the PI before publishing.

## File naming and document hygiene

- All shared documents live in the RIPLRT shared drive (or the project repo for code). Even a first solo draft is created in the shared space — transparency and open collaboration are foundational.
- Follow the **file-naming convention** for each folder. Where a folder has a `README` describing its naming pattern, follow it; if one is missing, ask the project lead or PI and add one.
- Use ISO dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), no spaces (use `_` or `-`), and meaningful, sortable names. Example: `2026-06-01_PR-sporecast_analysis-v3.qmd`.

## Meeting cadence

- **Weekly pod check-ins** keep projects moving; use the weekly agenda template.
- **A recurring group huddle** ("RIPLRT Wins & Roadblocks") builds identity across members on different datasets.
- **One-on-one mentoring meetings** run biweekly (see @sec-mentoring).
- Day, time, and frequency adapt to members' real availability; keep your availability current so scheduling is honest.

Every meeting has an **agenda in advance** and **notes + action items after** (owner + due date), stored in the tracked tool. No agenda, no meeting; no notes, no follow-through.

## Digital body language

Tone is hard to read in text, and the absence of cues (face, voice, pauses) means people fill gaps with assumptions — usually negative ones. **Digital body language** is the set of signals our written communication sends. We are deliberate about it.

**Practices we use:**

- **Acknowledge receipt.** A quick "got it, will reply by Thursday" prevents silence from reading as dismissal.
- **Match channel to weight.** Hard or sensitive conversations move to a call. Bad news and conflict are not for chat threads.
- **Be generous in interpretation, careful in expression.** Assume good intent when reading; reduce ambiguity when writing.
- **Mind asynchronous timing.** A message sent at 11 PM should not imply a reply is expected at 11 PM. Use scheduled send or a "no rush" note. Respect availability and time off.
- **Watch the curtness gap.** Brevity that feels efficient to the sender can read as cold to the receiver. A little warmth (a greeting, a thank-you, a sign-off) is not inefficiency; it's maintenance of trust.
- **Punctuation and response time carry meaning.** A one-word reply, a long delay, or a sudden formality shift all signal something. If you notice these in others, check in rather than assume; if you're sending them, consider what they convey.

::: {.callout-note}
## Read for signal, not just content
When a teammate's messages change — terser, slower, more formal, suddenly cc'ing others — treat it as information. It often means stress, confusion, or a problem surfacing. The right move is a kind, direct check-in ("Hey, want to hop on a quick call about this?"), not a tit-for-tat escalation in writing.
:::

## No-surprises communication

The single most important communication norm at RIPLRT: **no surprises.**

- If a deadline is at risk, say so *early* and propose a renegotiation — don't go silent and miss it.
- If an analysis isn't working, raise it before the meeting, not in front of the room cold.
- If you're overloaded, name it before it becomes a crisis.

Communicating a problem early is a sign of professionalism, not failure. The version of you that says "I'm going to be two days late, here's my plan" is far more trusted than the version that misses silently and explains afterward.
